The promise: simplifying the longest feedback loop in enterprise data

3: STORY: SELECT: who I am, and why this idea exists (keep it brief)
PhD: 350M-person graph identity system • 8-figure graph practice at DataStax • graph engine at AWS re:Invent
Land the line: "I live in the space where data meets real business decisions."
4: STORY: WITH: the origin story of this idea
Mount Washington, Seattle, with Matthias: why is it so hard for cross-functional teams to share an understanding of their data?
Conversation → outline → a year of writing → our O'Reilly book, The Practitioner's Guide to Graph Data
The book's argument: connect data across silos into a shared domain model and you see what was invisible (healthcare fraud, retail behavior chains, financial risk)
The book did well; people resonated. But the catch: it took 400 pages just to describe the collaboration, and teams found graph hard to adopt because everything converged on SQL
Two truths: connected data is where the value is • tooling has to meet engineers where they are
The AI wave forces the question of this talk: why does it still take weeks or months for that logic to reach production?
5: STORY: DESCRIBE: name the tension and the real problem [ANIMATION]
The workflow hasn't changed: agree on logic by screen-sharing SQL → buried in thousands of files → wait days, weeks, months for the dashboard
WHAT WORKS: the agreement. SQL is the shared language of trust between business and engineering.
WHAT DOESN'T: weeks to get a metric into operations • native graph tooling (400 pages; the world converged on SQL)
THE NEW PRESSURE: if SQL is the ubiquitous language of data, why weeks or months to production?
From the business' perspective, the problem isn't the query language…
[click] …the problem is the infrastructure and latency that come after it
Preview the answer: align at SQL that defines pipelines, database views, and production-ready endpoints automatically
AI automates the most mechanical parts of the analytics lifecycle, not to replace engineers or generate insights → a much shorter path from business logic to usable analytics
Tee up the open questions: where humans stay, where automation helps, why the most impactful AI may be the least flashy
6: STORY: LAG: the old playbook, one system [ANIMATION]
Start with a data problem, work backwards from the user experience to define infrastructure, APIs, data model; pick tools; plan volume, throughput, SLAs
Walk the cycle: 1 copy & replicate data → 2 build the model (repeat until good enough) → 3 build pipelines (until green) → 4 build APIs (until green) → 5 feedback loops (until minimum acceptable)
[click] Punchline: "all of that is per data system." (This is why engineers laugh or cry.)
7: STORY: LAG ×N: it multiplies, then it compounds
Multiply the whole cycle by every system: SQL, SparkSQL, Gremlin/Cypher, GraphQL
That alone isn't the kicker. You could parallelize it.
The real kicker is dependencies: move one computation from Postgres to Neptune = a coordinated rewrite across four (upstream feed, Postgres, Neptune, API layer)
Different owners, teams, backlogs: "You're not debugging code. You're negotiating calendars."
Land it: the old way doesn't just scale badly. It compounds badly.
Every cross-system optimization becomes a multi-team coordination project. That's the old way.
8: STORY: WHERE: the bottleneck isn't where you think
Sit with this: the agreement part works. Business and engineering screen-share SQL and agree.
The problem is everything after "yes, that's the right metric": infrastructure, latency, weeks or months to a dashboard, report, or email
This is the longest feedback loop in enterprise data work, and the one AI can actually shorten
Every leader's question: how do you use AI so DevOps and data engineers stay in the loop where their knowledge matters most?
POINT: we're stuck between three things: 1 connect data across silos • 2 with tools engineers can adopt • 3 figure out where AI fits (speed, trust, security, observability)
9: HIDDEN SLIDE • STORY: PARTITION BY: the silo problem (its three points are now said on slide 8)
Scale means throughput AND working with human minds across siloed architectures
Connecting silos = better insight and visibility into gaps, but graph isn't approachable; talent, compliance, auditors all speak SQL
Mixing data across silos is a major security implementation that touches every team
"If you're sitting in this room, you're probably living some version of it right now."
10: STORY: CREATE VIEW: the answer. Humans above the line, AI below, and the line is SQL.
Ask it: where are the humans in the loop, and where is AI?
After a decade on this: SQL is the natural collaboration point for both the "what" and the "how"
In the era of AI you still start with a data problem, build the domain model, design the UX with data, work backwards. That's the human understanding of the business.
Line to land: "if you are not adding AI into your stack to help initiatives that bring higher ROI to the company, then you are building side projects for fun."
THESIS: "We're proposing that the line is in SQL." Here's why:
Data engineers still analyze, build models, measure accuracy, repeat. That loop is human work: judgment, edge cases, domain fluency from sitting with compliance, product, ops.
The output of that loop is SQL, yesterday, today, tomorrow; reviewable for security, HIPAA, EU AI Act, GDPR
Yes, AI writes the SQL, but there's a moment of review: only pass if people say go. "That's how you make room for ethics in your builds."
Once a human approves the SQL, AI automates everything below the line: pipelines, APIs, feedback loops, infrastructure, deployment, monitoring
TRANSITION: "Think about what that does for your team."
11: STORY: GROUP BY: what your teams get back
Data engineers: plumbers → engineers. They translate business problems into data problems. "AI can't sit in a room and get five executives to agree on what 'churn' means."
DevOps: hand-holding → standardization. Compaction, logs, audits, back pressure, and finally time for R&D.
The relationship: friction → trust. DevOps and data engineers get time to grab a beer and understand each other.
From almost twenty years in: technical problems almost never kill a data initiative. Teams not understanding each other does.
SQL fixes something technical AND something human
It looks like data mesh's promise (ownership, faster analytics, tighter collaboration), reached through workflow automation instead of org redesign
TRANSITION: two reasons SQL is a good bet for years, or decades
12: STORY: FULL OUTER JOIN: Reason 1. SQL balances the business.
Three groups must agree: domain experts and PMs • data engineers and scientists • DevOps (all of ops, MLOps included)
SQL is the one language all three read: experts check meaning, engineers check correctness, DevOps check stability (no 2 AM runaway query)
Nobody sets AI loose end to end. You need an observable, loggable point to measure budget, accuracy, security, compliance and governance.
You can audit, diff, test, and log SQL
POINT: SQL is human-readable, machine-parseable, and auditable at every level of the stack. Pipeline configs and IaC aren't where humans should collaborate.
13: STORY: COMMIT: Reason 2. Every hype wave pulls back to SQL.
Will this still matter in three years?
Walk the six waves: relational, object-oriented, MapReduce, NoSQL, graph (I was deep in it), AI/vector. Every one pulled back to SQL.
Land it: "The hypes come and go. SQL stays." When you build for enterprises, "you bet on patterns, not hypes."
TRANSITION: after the book, Matthias built tooling that makes this real, and we've used it together on real enterprise builds. Not a theory. Tested in production.
14: HIDDEN SLIDE • STORY: COMMIT: the durable pain is integration, not the AI
25 new LLMs next year, an order of magnitude more frameworks: that keeps moving
The durable pain: the right data, from the right sources, with the right access controls, in the right shape
That's what SQL as the collaboration point is designed to address
15: STORY: EXECUTE: proof. Same pattern, three industries.
BANKING (brownfield): 50+ service domain teams (payments, fraud, onboarding, lending). A data engineer per team, or a central queue? Neither works.
"That's the bottleneck we've been talking about for the last thirty minutes, multiplied by fifty."
The goal: empower fifty teams to build their own pipelines without a data engineer each, and without fifty slightly different versions of the same pipeline
Banking answer: every team already writes SQL → one standard platform, automation below the line. "Fifty teams, one platform, one shared language."
HEALTHCARE (running at scale): HIPAA, clinical data; not exotic data science, a "get the right data into the right shape and ship it" problem stuck in the bottleneck
TRAVEL (greenfield): where Matthias and I teamed up. A 70-year-old international network building a net-new product.
Travel question: building an analytics cloud from scratch in the age of AI, where do you put the humans and where do you let AI take over?
Travel answer: humans review and agree at the SQL layer; AI built 50–70 analytics APIs plus operational ones, no hand-building
Plug: follow the Substack for updates on the build

18: My arc: ~2 decades in graph. We were right about the insight: connected data produces better outcomes.
Learned the hard way (400 pages, years of builds): tooling has to meet engineers where they are, and that's SQL
AI is already changing data architecture. The question is how to best use human intelligence.
Humans: domain models, UX with data, the SQL that operationalizes insight • AI: everything below the SQL line
People payoff: data engineers go from pipeline plumbers to real engineers (the civil engineer designing the bridge, not the person handed a shovel)
Not turning them into data scientists: most enterprises need collaborative filtering, a random forest, and real engineers who ship
"I think it's at least a very promising path forward. And I'd love your help figuring out what we're missing."
